target.title: fix(publish): defer close-proof retries to proof lane
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #635's `retry_pr_close_coverage_proof` publisher loop: an immutable exact-result publisher cannot run the Codex-backed close-coverage proof, so replaying that same artifact repeatedly exhausts publication attempts and dead-letters it.

## Problem

The live incident left close-coverage retry artifacts in the publisher/DLQ path. The publisher has no proof credentials, whereas the bounded read-only `apply-proof` lane does. Replaying the immutable artifact cannot change that capability boundary.

## Implementation

- Persist a durable `deferred / close_coverage_deferred` publisher completion and let the existing proof-capable lane select it.
- Never route a deferred close recommendation directly.
- Preserve the old `refresh_required / close_coverage_retry` completion for an in-flight workflow that has new helper code but lacks the new workflow opt-in.
- Retain the source lease through the proof handoff, complete the command status as a completed review with explicit downstream proof gating, and accept only the exact trusted status-comment churn.
- Fail closed if the reviewed source revision, PR activity, or human activity changed; PATCH-style command-status updates match their raw `updated_at` and timeline `created_at` separately.
- Avoid hydration of issue timeline/status context for every ordinary apply: it is evaluated only for `retry_pr_close_coverage_proof`, fixing the real 20-case mock-GitHub CI regression on the first revision.

The durable queue already retains a first `permanent_failure / unknown_failure` completion as one pending retry. A new regression test pins that rolling-deployment safety: an old workflow YAML that runs newly merged publisher code cannot turn the temporary unknown completion into a dead letter before a current workflow run handles the deferred contract.

## Validation

- `pnpm run build`
- `pnpm run build:repair`
- `pnpm run build:dashboard`
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check <all touched files>`
- Focused `node --test` coverage for the trusted deferred status, source drift, close-coverage deferral, legacy compatibility, immutable handoff, and proposed-close selection.
- `git diff --check`
- Fresh GitHub Actions `pnpm check` on `d0c28ea6b0` — passed (10m 4s).

Focused checks passed. The regression tests prove both that an unchanged trusted command-status handoff reaches the bounded proof lane and that a title/body source edit is rejected before Codex proof or close work.

The stale first-revision `pnpm check` failure was investigated rather than waived: the new close-proof status helper evaluated `currentItemContext()` for unrelated ordinary applies, adding unexpected timeline calls to 20 mock-GitHub cases. Commit `d0c28ea6b0` guards that evaluation by action and adds the rolling-deploy queue regression test.

## Controlled Linux runtime proof

On 2026-07-17, a clean Docker-backed Crabbox local container (`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.60.0-noble`, Node `v24.15.0`, pnpm `11.10.0`) installed with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, built the TypeScript/dashboard targets, and ran the exact queue/apply-proof behavior. Lease `cbx_1b61620e9b7b` completed with exit code 0:

- `apply-decisions permits a trusted deferred close-proof command status through post-proof freshness`
- `apply-decisions rejects a source edit masked by a deferred close-proof status`
- `exact-review publication retains one unknown completion for a current-workflow retry`
- `exact event proof defers a close-coverage retry to the proof-capable apply lane`

Result: 4 passed, 0 failed. This is controlled Linux runtime evidence through the real built queue/apply boundaries; it does not claim a live GitHub publication or use a live GitHub write token.

## Persistent completion-contract integration proof

On 2026-07-17, a second clean Docker-backed Crabbox container (`cbx_bad10c4a5823`, `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.60.0-noble`) built the branch's repair target and started the real `dashboard/worker.ts` under `wrangler@4.107.0 dev --local --persist-to`. Its actual `ExactReviewQueue` Durable Object initialised a SQLite store.

To keep the canary isolated and avoid a GitHub or Cloudflare mutation, a redacted leased publication fixture was inserted into that local Durable Object store while the Worker was stopped. After restart, the real tuple-capability completion endpoint received the publisher wire contract:

```text
outcome=success
completion_kind=deferred
reason_code=close_coverage_deferred
```

It returned `{ ok: true, requeued: false }`. After another Worker restart against the same persisted directory, the live queue statistics were `completed_total: 1`, `retried_total: 0`, and `dead_letters_open: 0`; the publisher item had no remaining live or dead-letter row.

In the same built branch, the actual `event-apply-proof` module classified the sole `retry_pr_close_coverage_proof` outcome as `close_coverage_deferred` without requeueing the immutable publisher, while a verified `skipped_changed_since_review` result classified as `source_drift` and selected a fresh retry.

This is an isolated persisted Worker/queue integration proof of the completion contract and decision boundary. It deliberately does not claim the remaining hosted Actions properties: GitHub App token identity, real status-comment timing, or an actual publisher-to-proof-lane run. GitHub executes `repository_dispatch` from default `main`, and the publisher job explicitly checks out `main`, so an unmerged PR cannot be truthfully exercised by a normal live command.

Codex review closeout:

- `codex review --uncommitted` — clean after the rolling-deploy regression test.
- Final `codex review --base origin/main` at `d0c28ea6b0` — clean: “No actionable correctness issues.”

`actionlint` is not installed on this Windows host. A previous broad local Linux-container suite hit pre-existing CRLF Bash-fixture failures after Windows source sync (`pipefail\r`); this branch does not change `scripts/`, and the fresh native-Linux GitHub CI run passed.

## Risks and rollout

- The deferred path covers only the exact `retry_pr_close_coverage_proof` outcome. It does not automatically replay or alter existing DLQ rows.
- The proof lane remains bounded and read-only until its normal guarded apply step; no close is authorized by the publisher handoff itself.
- This touches `.github/workflows/sweep.yml`; GitHub workflow OAuth/token scope and the normal repository write-token behavior remain an operational risk to verify in a maintainer-owned hosted staging environment or through an explicitly accepted monitored rollout.

## Related

Fixes #635.

Related: #634, #641, and #651 (the separate, explicitly operator-invoked guarded DLQ recovery control). Land this producer-side prevention before using #651 for any recovery.

target.title: fix(memory-core): honor private-network settings for OpenAI-compatible embeddings
target.body:
Fixes #94166

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users selecting a configured OpenAI-compatible memory embedding provider could not consistently use its private endpoint policy. The embedding adapter ignored `models.providers.<id>.request.allowPrivateNetwork`, so configured private endpoints could remain blocked even when the provider explicitly allowed them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Memory embeddings now reuse the canonical provider request resolver and shared transport SSRF policy. Omitted policy trusts only the exact configured `baseUrl` origin, explicit `true` permits broader private-network requests, and explicit `false` disables exact-origin trust while preserving the independent fake-IP DNS policy used by Clash, Surge, and sing-box networks. Explicit denial also prevents configured local-service acquisition before the guarded request.

This refresh rebases the existing fix onto current `main`, preserves the newer resolved-SecretRef boundary, and adapts regression coverage to the current embedding adapter without restoring the removed internal test export.

## User Impact

Operators can use configured OpenAI-compatible memory embedding endpoints with the same private-network policy as other provider HTTP requests. Trust remains scoped by scheme, hostname, and port unless broader access is explicitly enabled; remote overrides on another origin do not inherit configured-origin trust.

No schema, migration, dependency, lockfile, gateway, channel, session, or non-memory provider behavior is changed.

## Evidence

Current conflict-resolution head: `40f6d365172a11ddaf10a863fff899829691815a`

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts` — 1 file passed, 31 tests passed.
- Regression proof includes configured-origin success with omitted policy, explicit opt-in success, explicit-denial blocking before local-service acquisition, remote-origin isolation, canonical resolver input, and preservation of fake-IP DNS policy under explicit denial.
- The fake-IP composition test failed before the final review fix because the shared transport resolver was never called, then passed after explicit denial was narrowed to disabling exact-origin trust only.
- `pnpm check:test-types` — passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.ts src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts` — passed.
- `git diff --check` — passed.
- `codex review --base origin/main` found the fake-IP policy regression described above; it was fixed and covered by the failing-first regression test.

The prior PR head `1dc7c67289f6ad6dbd0e129f3fbd85220ad5d12c` had green hosted CI and a real `openclaw memory status --deep --json` FastEmbed proof for omitted, explicit-false, and explicit-true policy states. That full CLI/FastEmbed proof was not rerun on this conflict-resolution head; current-head verification used the focused real HTTP test server and static/type checks listed above.

The repository changed-check wrapper attempted Blacksmith Testbox delegation, but the local `crabbox` binary failed its basic sanity check. The trusted-source fallback ran locally. Its max-lines ratchet could not execute because the host Git lacks `git cat-file --batch -z`; hosted CI remains authoritative for that gate.

target.title: fix: guarded fetch falls back to IPv6 when IPv4 is unreachable
target.body:
Closes #87763

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where guarded provider requests on dual-stack hosts can fail when IPv4 is unreachable even though IPv6 is available.

## Why This Change Was Made

Single-address pinned lookups remain IPv4-only when IPv4 records exist, preserving the behavior introduced for #80078. All-record lookups used by Node/Undici Happy Eyeballs now receive the complete SSRF-validated, IPv4-first pinned record set, so IPv6 remains available as a fallback. Explicit-family and hostname-fallback behavior are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on networks where a provider's IPv4 route is unavailable but IPv6 works can complete guarded provider requests without disabling DNS pinning or weakening resolved-address checks.

## Evidence

- Updated `src/infra/net/ssrf.pinning.test.ts` proves:
  - repeated single-address lookups stay on IPv4;
  - `{ all: true }` returns IPv4 and IPv6 in IPv4-first order;
  - explicit family 6 still returns IPv6.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- Independent live observation on Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, Node v24.15.0, OpenClaw 2026.5.26: direct Node fetch used working IPv6 while guarded fetch timed out on IPv4; retaining the validated IPv6 candidate restored a real OpenRouter provider request.
- CI: pending on this draft PR.
- Not tested: current `main` has not been rerun live against the asymmetric OpenRouter route; the live proof used the shipped 2026.5.26 code path.

AI-assisted: Codex helped diagnose, implement, and review this change. I reviewed the code and understand the behavior. Session logs are not attached because the diagnostic conversation contained credentials; all evidence above is sanitized.

target.title: fix(slack): stabilize tool-result reaction tests
target.body:
Related: #109910

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where five Slack reaction assertions in the tool-result suite intermittently observed zero reaction calls during the full Slack test lane, despite the underlying turn reaching the reply resolver. The failures reproduced on clean `main` in 2 of 3 full-suite runs.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Slack lane runs non-isolated in one worker. Its global mock client survives file-level module resets, but the reaction delegates remained closed over whichever test file first created that client. Suite ordering therefore routed reaction calls into stale mocks. The helper now rebinds those delegates to the active file's hoisted mocks, and terminal reaction tests opt into the existing durable-ingress lifecycle so assertions await dispatch completion instead of timer turns.

No production runtime behavior changes. AI-assisted; implementation and failure mechanism reviewed directly.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Slack CI now reports reaction behavior deterministically, including silent turns and dispatch failures.

## Evidence

- Baseline: unchanged `main` passed once, then failed all five named reaction tests on the second full Slack run (1,881 passed / 5 failed).
- Focused: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/slack/src/monitor.tool-result.test.ts` — 29/29 passed.

target.title: Plugin UI: add scoped action bridge for sandboxed tabs
target.body:
## Summary

- extend the merged `surface: "tab"` descriptor with an explicit `sessionActions` allowlist and separate `allowChatNavigation` capability
- connect opaque sandboxed plugin tabs to the authenticated parent with a per-frame `MessagePort`
- pass the active Control UI session key and known context-window size through the existing `plugins.sessionAction` path
- document the frame protocol and security boundary

## What Problem This Solves

#107323 provides tab discovery, scope visibility, sandboxing, and a read-only `GET`/`HEAD` cookie grant. Real plugin pages still need a narrow way to perform explicit mutations and return users to chat. Without that bridge, Hands Free settings can render but cannot save, test, pair, forget, configure audio/output, or deploy; Session Search can render results but cannot inject/resume sessions or navigate back to the resulting chat.

This is the replacement candidate for #80388, scoped only to those missing capabilities. It intentionally does **not** add `openMode`, generic parent fetch, generic mutation cookies, parallel registration/list RPCs, or bearer-token access from the frame.

## Security model

- the parent fixes the plugin ID from the active descriptor
- only descriptor-allowlisted action IDs are dispatched
- existing action-declared operator scopes and payload/result schemas remain authoritative at the Gateway
- the parent supplies the active session; frame-provided session targets are ignored for action dispatch
- chat navigation is an independent opt-in capability
- the sandboxed frame receives neither the Gateway bearer token nor a generic HTTP proxy

## Evidence

Migrated local Hands Free and Session Search plugin builds use this contract. Hands Free maps its seven mutations to explicit admin-scoped actions and uses one-time short-lived GET URLs for large audio/archive results. Session Search maps injection/resume targeting to a write-scoped action and uses the navigation capability to return to chat.

Focused validation completed before opening this PR:

- 31 core contract/registry/Gateway/UI bridge tests passed
- 14 Session Search plugin tests passed, including direct action dispatch and context-window enforcement
- 2 Hands Free Playwright browser tests passed, including the origin-isolated iframe path and mutation dispatch
- SDK surface report, formatting, diff checks, syntax checks, and max-lines ratchet passed

Keep #80388 open until this replacement has passed CI and compatibility review.

target.title: fix(infra): use bigint stats when comparing session store identity
target.body:
Fixes #110123

## Problem

On filesystems with inode numbers above 2^53 (e.g. bcachefs), `resolveSessionStorePathRelationship()` compares file identity using non-bigint `fs.statSync()`. JS number rounding makes distinct files report identical inodes (at ~8.6e17 adjacent doubles are 128 apart), so different agents' session stores are classified as the same file reachable via different paths. Startup migrations defer with "aliased store" warnings, and on 2026.7.1 — where these migrations are fatal — the gateway refuses to start. `doctor --fix` cannot resolve it because no actual filesystem aliases exist.

## Change

Pass `{ bigint: true }` to both `statSync` calls. `FileIdentityStat` is already typed `number | bigint` and `sameStatValue()` already coerces mixed comparisons, so no changes needed in `@openclaw/fs-safe`.

## Verification

- Reproduced on a bcachefs root (see issue for real stat output showing 3-way inode collisions across agent stores).
- Applied this exact change to an installed 2026.7.1 dist on the affected machine: all `Deferred session key migration in aliased store` failures disappeared and the gateway started cleanly; without it, startup crash-loops.
- Other `sameFileIdentity` call sites compare pre/post-open stats of the same path, where rounding is consistent — unaffected.

A unit test would need `fs.statSync` mocking through the exported migration entry points since the helper is module-private; happy to add one if you point me at the preferred harness.

target.title: fix(cli): deliver pre-tool assistant blocks durably
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

CLI-backed runtimes can emit substantive assistant text before tool calls, but that text currently only reaches transient progress previews. The durable channel reply contains only the short terminal CLI result, so operators can miss findings or direct questions.

Fixes #110067.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Reuse the CLI parser's existing pre-tool text classification instead of adding a second parser or provider-specific path.
- Route completed pre-tool assistant blocks through the existing block-reply handler only when block streaming is enabled.
- Drain and force-flush each queued assistant block before tool progress so the channel preserves source order.
- Preserve the existing ephemeral preamble item-event bridge.
- Leave block-streaming-disabled behavior unchanged, including the existing final-result path.

## User Impact

With block streaming enabled, CLI users receive substantive pre-tool assistant prose as durable channel messages instead of losing it when the final CLI result is only a short wrap-up. Tool progress remains ordered after the prose, and the final CLI result is still returned normally.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test covering durable pre-tool delivery, delivery before tool-start progress, and preservation of the final CLI result.
- `oxlint` passed for both changed files.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- OpenClaw `autoreview` completed cleanly with no accepted/actionable findings (0.9 confidence).
- Focused Vitest and changed-file checks: pending GitHub Actions because the local checkout could not fetch current `main` over the shell network.

## AI Assistance

This change was implemented with Codex assistance. Codex inspected the issue and current source path, authored the narrow implementation and regression test, ran formatting/static checks, and completed the repository's structured autoreview. No agent transcript is attached.

target.title: improve: compose conversation tools in Code Mode
target.body:
Related: #109288
Follow-up to #109813

## What Problem This Solves

Code Mode knew exact result shapes only for tools that declared them. The conversation address workflow still appeared output-unknown, so models often spent extra inspection turns between listing a destination and sending or awaiting a reply. In live runs, some providers also wrapped an unknown final reply incorrectly.

## Why This Change Was Made

The conversation tools now reuse the existing Gateway list, send, and turn result schemas as their single output-contract owner. Complete trusted output hints get a separate 600-character/depth-6 budget while input hints keep their existing 300-character/depth-4 budget; catalog-wide, property, union, and trust caps remain unchanged. Unknown final calls also receive explicit raw-first guidance.

Normal tool policy, hooks, approvals, and remote MCP/client trust boundaries are unchanged. This PR is AI-assisted; I reviewed the implementation and understand the ownership and validation paths.

## User Impact

Agents can list external conversations, select a returned conversation reference, and send or await a correlated reply in one Code Mode execution. This reduces model round-trips, latency, and token use without loosening tool execution policy.

## Evidence

- Live real-Agent matrix: OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages, and Google Generative AI; four validated operations (lookup, send, correlated turn, absent-target recovery); 72 tools with adversarial decoys.
- Declared contracts: 12/12 correct, 26 turns, 14 Code Mode calls, 68.858 seconds aggregate latency, 36,095 input tokens, 1,966 output tokens, zero decoy calls.
- Schema-stripped baseline: 11/12 correct, 37 turns, 25 Code Mode calls, 99.980 seconds aggregate latency, 61,535 input tokens, 2,796 output tokens, one decoy call.
- Improvement: 30% fewer turns, 44% fewer Code Mode calls, 31% less aggregate latency, and 41% fewer input tokens.
- Stress: 36/36 declared-contract runs passed across all providers and operations over three repetitions; zero decoy calls.
- Focused tests: 171 passed across schema hints, Gateway agent schemas, conversation tools, Tool Search, and Code Mode runtime.
- Packaged build passed. Changed checks passed, including core/core-test typechecks, changed-file lint, import-cycle and boundary guards.
- Documentation checks passed: MDX over 737 files and 6,058 internal links with zero broken links.
- Renderer setup microbenchmark: 0.700 ms per 72-tool catalog render on Node 26.5.0. That Node build does not expose a `node --benchmark` option, so the measurement used `node:perf_hooks`.
- Autoreview: no accepted/actionable findings, overall confidence 0.94.
- Blacksmith Testbox warmup timed out before lease allocation; repository policy permitted the trusted-source local fallback used for build and changed checks.

target.title: fix(e2e): keep phase log tails UTF-8 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`PhaseRunner` (`scripts/e2e/parallels/phase-runner.ts`) keeps a bounded in-memory log tail per phase (`appendTextTail`) and writes that tail to stderr when a phase fails. The bound is applied as a raw byte cut — `Buffer.from(combined).subarray(-tailBytes).toString("utf8")` — so when the retained window starts in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character (emoji/CJK in test output), the diagnostics tail begins with U+FFFD replacement characters.

This is the same bug family as merged #109669 (`scripts/e2e/lib/text-file-utils.mjs`) and open sibling #109670 (`scripts/e2e/parallels/host-server.ts`); `phase-runner.ts` is the remaining byte-based tail decoder in the parallels harness. The three PRs touch separate files and are not stacked; any order merges cleanly.

## Why This Change Was Made

#109669 introduced `decodeUtf8Tail`, which drops leading UTF-8 continuation bytes before decoding a truncated window. This PR exports that helper and reuses it in `appendTextTail`, so the byte cap stays unchanged while the emitted tail always starts on a character boundary. The change is three lines in prod code plus a focused regression test.

Root cause on `main` (`scripts/e2e/parallels/phase-runner.ts:18`): the byte cut from `subarray(-tailBytes)` can start on a UTF-8 continuation byte, and `toString("utf8")` replaces each orphaned continuation byte with U+FFFD.

Deliberately out of scope: `scripts/e2e/parallels/filesystem.ts` has a similar byte-window read, but its only consumer is a regex scan (`extractLastOpenClawVersionFromLog`) whose ASCII pattern cannot straddle a character boundary, so a partial leading character there has no observable effect.

## User Impact

Maintainers reading failed E2E phase output get a clean log tail instead of leading mojibake whenever multibyte text (emoji in test names/output, CJK) crosses the 512 KiB tail cutoff.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof against the production `PhaseRunner` on `main` (driver: construct with a 128-byte cap, `append()` 134 bytes containing an emoji positioned so the byte window starts one byte into it, fail the phase, capture stderr):

Before (origin/main):

```
[phase log tail truncated to last 128 bytes]
���yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy
contains U+FFFD replacement char: true
```

After (this branch):

```
[phase log tail truncated to last 128 bytes]
yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy
contains U+FFFD replacement char: false
```

Regression coverage: `test/scripts/parallels-phase-runner.test.ts` drives the real class through a failing phase and asserts the stderr tail (1) contains no U+FFFD when the byte cut splits a character, (2) keeps the full emoji tail when the cut lands on a character boundary, (3) leaves short logs untruncated.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/parallels-phase-runner.test.ts` — 3/3 pass on this branch; the split-character test fails on unpatched `phase-runner.ts` (control-red verified by reverting the prod file to `origin/main`).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/e2e-text-file-utils.test.ts` — pass (sibling helper tests unaffected by the new export).
- `oxfmt --check` on all touched files — clean; `oxlint` on touched files — 0 findings; `tsgo --noEmit -p tsconfig.scripts.json` — no errors in touched files (pre-existing `packages/net-policy` errors come from a stale local `ipaddr.js@1.9.1`, unrelated).
- `git diff --check` — clean.

target.title: fix(voice-call): ngrok tunnels no longer survive cleanup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where voice-call could release ngrok process ownership while the process was still running when it ignored `SIGTERM`. This affected both normal runtime cleanup and the 30-second startup-timeout path, where a surviving process could keep an external tunnel active after stop completed or startup failed.

## Why This Change Was Made

A module-local ngrok termination helper now waits two seconds for graceful termination, escalates to `SIGKILL`, and waits for the child `close` event. A final one-second fallback keeps ownership release bounded even if close is never observable. Both successful stop and startup timeout use the helper; the change adds no configuration or API surface.

## User Impact

Voice-call no longer leaves a SIGTERM-resistant ngrok tunnel behind after either runtime shutdown or startup failure. Both paths retain finite upper bounds, so an unresponsive child cannot make cleanup wait forever.

## Evidence

- Current-main reproductions: a real executable named `ngrok` ignored `SIGTERM`; the old `stop()` returned with its PID still alive, and the old startup-timeout path rejected with its PID still alive one second later.
- Standalone production-path proof: `startTunnel` spawned a real ngrok-named child; the child was alive before cleanup, recorded `SIGTERM`, and was dead when `stop()` returned after about 2.0 seconds.
- Standalone startup-timeout proof: a real ngrok-named child emitted no recognized URL, ignored `SIGTERM`, and was dead before `startTunnel` rejected after about 32.0 seconds.
- `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-voice-call.config.ts extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.process.test.ts` — 2 files passed, 21 tests passed.
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.ts extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.process.test.ts` — passed.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.ts extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.process.test.ts` — passed.
- Fresh same-problem scan found no equivalent open PR. #109416 changes ngrok startup-timer bookkeeping but does not add bounded signal escalation or child reaping.
- The live proof does not contact the ngrok service or use credentials; a real OS child reproduces the targeted SIGTERM-resistant shutdown behavior. Broader extension TypeScript/check-changed coverage remains with hosted CI.

target.title: feat(comfy): dynamic aspect ratio → width/height injection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves Resolves a problem where `image_generate` requests to a Comfy-backed model with `size` or `aspectRatio` set were silently ignored: ComfyUI workflow JSON bakes width/height into the graph, and OpenClaw had no way to route a requested size/aspect ratio into that graph, so every Comfy image came out at whatever dimensions the workflow author hard-coded, regardless of what the caller asked for. ## Why This Change Was Made Comfy now always advertises `supportsSize`/`supportsAspectRatio` as supported, and lets operators opt a workflow in by mapping a `dimensions` block (width/height node IDs) in the plugin config; at generation time, a requested `size` or `aspectRatio` is computed and injected into those nodes before the workflow runs. This is intentionally minimal-scope and stays entirely inside `extensions/comfy/`: capabilities are a **static** object, not a per-request resolver, so no core `ImageGenerationProvider` type, `normalization.ts`/`runtime.ts`, or `plugin-sdk` changes were needed. When `dimensions` isn't mapped (or the requested value can't be parsed), Comfy falls back to the workflow's own baked-in defaults and reports that back via `metadata.dimensionsApplied: false` instead of silently pretending the request was honored. ## User Impact Operators who add a `dimensions` block to their Comfy image workflow config can now get the `size`/`aspectRatio` they request from `image_generate` actually reflected in the output. Operators who don't configure `dimensions` see no behavior change (the workflow's existing hard-coded dimensions are used, as before), but now get an explicit `dimensionsApplied: false` signal in the result metadata instead of a silent no-op. ## Evidence - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/comfy/image-generation-provider.test.ts` — 36/36 passed, including a new `describe("dimensions")` block covering explicit size injection, aspect-ratio calculation, size/aspectRatio precedence, custom `baseSize`, no-config fallback, malformed-value fallback, and static capability advertisement (full list under Tests below). - `pnpm tsgo:extensions` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` — clean, no type errors. - `oxlint` on all changed files — clean. - `git diff --check` — clean (no whitespace errors). - Real end-to-end chat log + generated images below, showing `image_generate` honoring an explicit size (`640x960`) and an aspect ratio (`3:2`) against a live Comfy workflow.

New behavior is covered by the focused unit tests above.)* ## Changes - **`extensions/comfy/workflow-runtime.ts`** - Added `ComfyDimensionConfig` type + `resolveComfyDimensionConfig()` — reads the `dimensions` block off capability config (`widthNodeId`/`heightNodeId` required, `widthInputName`/`heightInputName`/`baseSize` optional), returns `undefined` when not configured - Added `calculateDimensions()` — parses an explicit `size` (`"512x768"`) directly, or derives width/height from `aspectRatio` (`"16:9"`) using a configurable base resolution (default 1024px), long edge = `baseSize`, short edge rounded to the nearest 64px - `runComfyWorkflow()` now accepts `size`/`aspectRatio`, injects them into the configured width/height nodes when possible, and returns `dimensionsApplied: boolean` - **`extensions/comfy/image-generation-provider.ts`** - `capabilities.generate`/`capabilities.edit` now statically set `supportsSize: true, supportsAspectRatio: true` (always advertised, regardless of config) - Passes `size`/`aspectRatio` through to `runComfyWorkflow()` - When a `size`/`aspectRatio` was requested, echoes `metadata.dimensionsApplied` from the workflow-runtime result so callers can tell whether the override was actually applied or the workflow's defaults were used instead - **`extensions/comfy/openclaw.plugin.json`** - Added a `dimensions` config object (`widthNodeId`, `heightNodeId` required; `widthInputName`, `heightInputName`, `baseSize` optional) to both the root and the `image` capability schema, matching how every other per-capability key is already duplicated - **`extensions/comfy/image-generation-provider.test.ts`** - New `describe("dimensions")` block: explicit size injection, aspect-ratio calculation (rounded to 64px), size-over-aspectRatio precedence, custom `baseSize`, no-config fallback, malformed-value fallback, and static capability advertisement regardless of config - **`docs/providers/comfy.md`** - Documented the `dimensions` config block and its no-op/fallback behavior when unconfigured No core (`src/image-generation/**`) or `plugin-sdk` files change. ## Configuring Add a `dimensions` block to your Comfy image workflow config pointing at the node(s) that control output size: ```json "image": { "workflowPath": "...", "promptNodeId": "42", "dimensions": { "widthNodeId": "10", "heightNodeId": "10", "baseSize": 768 } } ``` - `widthNodeId` / `heightNodeId`: node IDs in your workflow JSON (can be the same node for joint width/height inputs) - `widthInputName` / `heightInputName`: input field names within those nodes (defaults: `"width"`, `"height"`) - `baseSize`: base resolution for aspect-ratio calculation, defaults to 1024. Use 512 for SD 1.5, 768 for SDXL, etc. ## Backwards compatibility Falls back cleanly — no config or request changes needed: 1. No `size`/`aspectRatio` on the request → dimension logic skipped entirely, no `dimensionsApplied` metadata 2. `size`/`aspectRatio` provided but no `dimensions` config → no injection, workflow unchanged, `dimensionsApplied: false` 3. Malformed `size`/`aspectRatio` value → `calculateDimensions()` returns `undefined`, no injection, `dimensionsApplied: false` 4. `size` takes precedence over `aspectRatio` when both are provided ## Tests - Explicit size injection into configured nodes - Calculated dimensions from aspect ratio (16:9 at base 1024 = 1024x576) - Size precedence over aspectRatio when both provided - Custom `baseSize` respected - Fallback (`dimensionsApplied: false`) when no `dimensions` config is present - Fallback when the requested size is malformed - Capabilities statically report `supportsSize`/`supportsAspectRatio: true` regardless of `dimensions` config

target.title: fix(active-memory): honor abortSignal during recall cleanup retry delays
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`cleanupActiveMemoryRecallSession` in `extensions/active-memory/recall-run.ts` retries session-artifact cleanup on a `[0, 50, 250]ms` schedule using bare `node:timers/promises` sleeps. The outer `runRecallSubagent` already accepts `params.abortSignal` (wired to the real controller in `recall.ts`) and honors it everywhere else, but the cleanup retry loop never received it — a cancelled recall still waited out the remaining backoff schedule inside the `finally` chain, and a late `AbortError` risked masking the main outcome.

Honest scope note: the absolute latency at stake is ~300ms. The value here is contract consistency — every other stage of the recall already honors the same signal, and cancellation during cleanup now returns promptly without being misreported as a cleanup failure.

## Why This Change Was Made

`node:timers/promises` `setTimeout` natively supports `{ signal }`, so the cleanup params simply thread `abortSignal` through and pass it to the sleep. An abort rejection returns early instead of throwing: the call site's `.catch` logs "failed to clean up recall session" and rethrows, and a cancelled cleanup is not a failure — letting the AbortError propagate there would both misreport it and risk masking the main-flow outcome in the `finally` chain. Non-abort errors (including the initial attempt at `delayMs: 0`, which always runs) keep the exact previous behavior.

## Changes

- Add optional `abortSignal` to the cleanup params; pass it to the backoff sleep via the native `{ signal }` option (zero new dependencies).
- Return early on abort; rethrow anything else unchanged. Pass `params.abortSignal` at the recall call site.
- Regression test: cleanup mock always rejects, the recall's own 20ms watchdog aborts during the first 50ms backoff; asserts exactly one cleanup attempt, sub-300ms wall clock, and no spurious cleanup-failure warning.

## User Impact

Cancelling or timing out a recall now tears down promptly instead of lingering through the remaining cleanup backoff, and cancellation is no longer logged as a cleanup failure.

## Evidence

Exact head: `d51b8d0fe7cf1d04efef9d3c835eb9a44141d005`.

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/active-memory/index.test.ts   (Node 24)
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  175 passed (175)
```

The new test drives the recall's real watchdog (`timeoutMs: 20`) as the abort source — same controller object an external cancel would trip. Against the pre-change implementation it fails deterministically: cleanup runs the full 3-attempt schedule (≥300ms) and the cleanup-failure warning fires despite the abort. Must-not-fire paths are covered by the existing "retries transient cleanup failures" (2 attempts, success, no warning) and "retries exhausted" (3 attempts + warning) tests, which still pass unchanged.

`oxlint` clean on both changed files; `tsgo` extensions project reports no errors in active-memory files.

## Intentionally out of scope

- If the abort lands during a post-failure backoff, the session artifact may remain on disk without a warning — the accepted cost of cancellation; the common path is covered by the unconditional first attempt.
- No change to the retry schedule, attempt counts, or cleanup failure reporting for real errors.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): cancel unread response body in crabline injection
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109992

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the `postCrablineInbound()` error path. When a Crabline inbound injection returns a non-ok HTTP status, the response body ReadableStream is now explicitly cancelled before throwing the error, preventing an unread stream resource leak.

**What NOT changed**: No change to the happy path — successful responses still pass through to the complete handler as before. No change to the Crabline injection logic, request construction, or error message format. No new dependencies added.

**Why NOT changed**: The body cancel is only needed before throwing, since the stream becomes unreachable after the throw. On success the body is not consumed by this function — the entire response is forwarded — so no cancel is required on the ok path.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — the pattern `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is a standard no-op on success and a no-throw guard on failure. It affects only the single error path in `crabline-transport.ts`. Zero risk of regression on the ok path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a Crabline inbound injection HTTP request returns a non-ok response (e.g., 502, 400), the response body stream is left unread, causing a potential resource leak (unconsumed ReadableStream). Node.js will emit a warning for unconsumed response bodies in future versions.

**Root Cause**: `postCrablineInbound()` throws immediately in the `if (!response.ok)` branch without cancelling the unread response body, leaving the stream open for garbage collection to clean up — which is non-deterministic and can retain buffers until GC runs.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the error path to eagerly release the stream. The `cancel()` method (Fetch API standard) releases the stream's resources. The `?.` optional chaining guards against a null body (e.g., 204 No Content responses or server errors that omit a body). The `.catch()` ensures that a double-cancel or rejection from the stream implementation does not propagate.

## Evidence

**Real behavior demonstrated**: Executed `response.body?.cancel()` before `throw` with mocked body objects that simulate the exact conditions of the Crabline transport error path. All four edge cases verified with observed terminal output.

**Exact commands run after this patch:**

```bash
npx tsx scripts/evidence-crabline.ts
```

**After-fix evidence:**

```
--- Body cancel before throw ---
Body cancelled before throw: YES ✅
Error: Crabline injection failed (502)

--- Cancel rejection handled ---
Cancel rejection suppressed: ✅
Error: Crabline injection failed (400)

--- Null body safe ---
Null body cancel: safe ✅

--- Double cancel safe ---
Double cancel: safe ✅ (n=2)

COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0
```

**Observed results after the fix**:
1. **Body canceled before throw** — `body.cancel()` called, cancellation flag set to `YES`, then `Error("Crabline injection failed (502)")` thrown. Confirms the cancel-before-throw ordering is correct.
2. **Cancel rejection handled** — When `body.cancel()` rejects (e.g., stream already errored), the `.catch(() => undefined)` suppresses it. Error propagates normally afterward.
3. **Null body safe** — Optional chaining `body?.cancel()` short-circuits on null/undefined body, no `TypeError` thrown. Relevant for HTTP 204 No Content or omitted body responses.
4. **Double cancel safe** — Calling `body.cancel()` twice is idempotent. No unhandled rejection.

**What was not tested**: Real Crabline server end-to-end injection (requires live adapter credentials and a running Crabline adapter). The demo covers the exact code contract: it exercises the same `body.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` pattern with the same error-propagation semantics as the production code path.

## Tests and validation

- `scripts/evidence-crabline.ts` — TypeScript demo exercising the `body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` pattern with mocked body objects, covering cancel-before-throw, cancel rejection, null body, and double cancel.
- `docs/.local/pr-109992/verify.log` — terminal session capture via `script -q` containing `COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0`.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

Related: #89491

*AI-assisted (approved by Peter)*

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users behind Clash, Surge, sing-box, or similar fake-IP proxy DNS would have OpenAI OAuth token exchange and refresh rejected when `auth.openai.com` resolved into the RFC 2544 benchmark range or IPv6 unique-local range.

## Summary

**What**: Cancel unread HTTP response body before throwing on non-ok status in Vault secret resolver.

**Why**: Without body cancellation, Vault error responses (403, 404) leave a dangling stream that wastes memory and can cause connection stalls in serverless environments.

**What changed / NOT changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before both throw statements in `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` and `readVaultSecret`. NOT changed: any error handling logic, logging, or response processing for ok responses.

**merge-risk**: Low. The change is 2 lines, guarded by optional chaining (`?.`) for null-body safety and `.catch()` for cancellation-rejection safety. No impact on the happy path (ok responses are unchanged). Existing callers observe no behavioral difference except reduced resource leaks on error paths.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When Vault returns a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 403, 404), the response body stream is left unread and unconsumed. This leaks memory and wastes bandwidth, and can also cause hanging connections in serverless/runtime environments that expect the body to be consumed or cancelled before the response goes out of scope.

**Root Cause**: The two code paths (`resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` and `readVaultSecret`) throw immediately on `!response.ok` without cancelling or reading the response body, leaving the stream dangling.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing on non-ok responses. The optional chaining safely handles null/undefined body, and the `.catch()` silently swallows any cancellation error (e.g., network glitch mid-cancel).

**Problem**: When downloading a Google-generated video fails with an HTTP error status, the response body stream remains unread, causing a resource leak.

**Root Cause**: The `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` function in `extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts` throws on `!response.ok` without cancelling the response body stream. The unread stream lingers until GC.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the throw, matching the pattern used in google-oauth provider.

**What changed**: One line added before the throw in `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` to cancel the response body stream.

**What NOT changed**: No changes to retry logic, error handling flow, response parsing, or any other part of the download pipeline. The fix is minimal and scoped strictly to stream cleanup on the error path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When downloading a generated video from Google's API returns an HTTP error (non-2xx, such as 400 Bad Request or 500 Internal Server Error), the response body stream is left unread, causing a resource/memory leak. The response body may contain error details but is never consumed, resulting in the Node.js HTTP client holding onto the socket until garbage collection. This can lead to resource exhaustion under repeated error conditions.

**Root Cause**: The `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` function in `extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts` (line 247) throws an error on `!response.ok` without cancelling the response body stream. The unread stream remains open until garbage collection, wasting memory and potentially keeping connections alive unnecessarily. **Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing the download error, ensuring the stream is properly closed. `backfillMatrixAuthDeviceIdAfterStartup` in `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/client/config.ts` checks `params.abortSignal` before and after the startup `whoami` call, and the production caller (`monitor/index.ts`) passes a real signal. An abort landing inside that backoff was only noticed after the sleep elapsed and a second `whoami` request had been issued.

## Why This Change Was Made

`retryMatrixAuthRequest` now accepts an optional `signal` and sleeps via `sleepWithAbort(ms, signal)` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/runtime-env` (same abort-aware helper as the merged #109604/#108561/#108408 sibling fixes). The backfill passes its `params.abortSignal` through `fetchMatrixWhoamiIdentity`. When the abort fires mid-backoff, the sleep's rejection propagates through `retryAsync`; a new `try/catch` in the backfill normalizes it to `undefined`, matching the contract of the existing post-`whoami` aborted checks. Non-abort failures still rethrow, and call sites that pass no signal (`resolveMatrixAuth`, password login) see zero behavior change — `sleepWithAbort(ms, undefined)` degenerates to the plain timer.

## Changes

- Thread an optional `signal` through `retryMatrixAuthRequest` and `fetchMatrixWhoamiIdentity`; backoff sleeps use `sleepWithAbort`.
- Pass `params.abortSignal` at the backfill call site; normalize abort rejection to `undefined` (no deviceId) while real network failures still propagate.
- Regression test: first `whoami` fails with a retryable `ECONNRESET`, abort fires inside the first 250ms backoff; asserts prompt `undefined`, exactly one request, and no deviceId persistence.

## User Impact

Stopping a Matrix account during startup no longer waits out the `whoami` retry backoff or issues a doomed second request; shutdown is prompt and no half-backfilled deviceId is persisted.

## Evidence

Exact head: `61bf06d32fffa32b079f9d641ef3203ec4de6c21`.

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/matrix/src/matrix/client.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  23 passed (23)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/matrix/src/matrix/monitor/index.test.ts
Tests  42 passed (42)
```

Same test against the pre-change implementation fails: the abort is ignored until the backoff elapses, a second `whoami` is issued, and the backfill rejects with a TypeError instead of returning `undefined` promptly.

`oxlint`/`oxfmt` clean on both changed files; `tsgo` extensions project reports no errors in matrix files.

## Intentionally out of scope

- The other `retryMatrixAuthRequest` call sites (`resolveMatrixAuth` startup whoami, password login) keep their current no-signal behavior; this PR only threads the signal where a real one already exists.
- No change to retry counts, delay bounds, or which errors are retryable.

target.title: fix(agents): honor abort signal during compaction summary retry backoff
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`summarizeChunks` in `src/agents/compaction.ts` retries summary generation via `retryAsync`. The mandatory `params.signal` is already forwarded to `generateSummary` and checked in `shouldRetry`, but the backoff sleep between attempts used the default unabortable timer. When a user cancels a session mid-compaction, the retry loop still waits out the full backoff (500ms–5s with jitter) before the abort is noticed.

## Why This Change Was Made

`retryAsync` accepts a custom `sleep`; this passes `sleepWithAbort(ms, params.signal)` (imported from `../infra/backoff.js`, the same source as `src/agents/api-key-rotation.ts`). An abort during the backoff now rejects the sleep, which propagates through `retryAsync` unwrapped — the existing `signal.aborted` checks in `summarizeChunks`/`summarizeWithFallbackResult` rethrow it, and the outermost compaction safeguard treats it exactly like the pre-existing abort path (cancel compaction, keep history). Only the response latency changes. This follows the same abort-aware-backoff pattern as the recently merged #109604 (telegram startup probe) and #108561 (discord gateway READY retry).

## Changes

- Pass `sleep: (ms) => sleepWithAbort(ms, params.signal)` to `retryAsync` in `summarizeChunks`.
- Add a regression test: `generateSummary` rejects once with a retryable error, the caller aborts 50ms into the ≥500ms backoff; asserts rejection with the abort reason, wall clock under 400ms, and exactly one `generateSummary` call.

## User Impact

Cancelling a session while compaction is retrying a summary now stops promptly instead of lingering through the remaining backoff.

## Evidence

Exact head: `fe96c958ae2800f35bdffae9eab907d21d04addf`.

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/compaction.summarize-fallback.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  5 passed (5)
```

Same suite against the pre-change implementation (file at `upstream/main`): the new test fails — the abort is ignored, the loop sleeps through the ~500ms backoff and calls `generateSummary` a second time (1130ms, rejects with the summarization error instead of the abort reason).

`oxlint` clean on both changed files; `tsgo` core project reports no errors in compaction files.

## Intentionally out of scope

- No change to retry counts, delay bounds, or the transient-error classification in `shouldRetry`.
- No change to the compaction safeguard's cancel handling; abort already landed there via other paths.

target.title: refactor(channels): move inbound turn execution into core
target.body:
Related: #109316

Follow-up to #109716.

## What Problem This Solves

Bundled message channels still owned the core execution half of inbound turns: session recording, dispatcher construction, durable-delivery handling, retry plumbing, reply pipelines, and final lifecycle callbacks. That kept deprecated low-level compatibility calls alive as internal architecture even after the marker sweep reached zero removable declarations.

## Why This Change Was Made

Core now owns the complete inbound turn lifecycle. Channel adapters return data-only turn plans containing normalized context plus transport delivery facts; the core runner performs recording, dispatch, retry, durable delivery, typing/reaction lifecycle composition, and finalization. Feishu, iMessage, Matrix, Mattermost, Microsoft Teams, QQBot, Signal, Telegram, and WhatsApp now use that path. Special native Mattermost interactions use the focused core reply seam instead of rebuilding lifecycle logic.

Shipped Plugin SDK declarations remain byte-compatible. A ratcheted guard rejects bundled production use of prepared-turn callbacks, pre-dispatch failure callbacks, and low-level dispatcher lifecycle calls.

## User Impact

No intended user-visible behavior change. External plugins keep the shipped compatibility window. Maintainers get transport-thinner channels, one core execution path, and a hard zero budget for internal deprecated channel lifecycle calls.

target.title: feat(memory-core): skip tool construction for dreaming narrative subagent runs (no-tools mode from #93756 review guidance)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Dreaming narrative subagent runs (light/deep/REM) generate 80–180 words of prose; `NARRATIVE_SYSTEM_PROMPT` explicitly prohibits tool use — yet every run still constructs the full tool/MCP/LSP surface before the model call.

This implements the fix requested by the maintainer review that closed the 60s→120s timeout-bump PRs ([#93756 closing comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/93756#issuecomment-4723436147)): *"an explicit no-tools subagent mode for these narrative-only runs, forwarded into the runner's existing empty-tool fast path."* The issue that tracked it (#92494) was closed without the mode being built; this PR builds it.

`disableTools: true` is threaded from the plugin call site through plugin→gateway→command→embedded-runner, landing in the runner's existing fast path (`resolveEmbeddedAttemptToolConstructionPlan` → `constructTools: false`; MCP/LSP bundle runtimes short-circuit).

## Changes

- **`dreaming-narrative.ts`**: `subagent.run({ …, disableTools: true })` (unconditional — narrative runs never need tools; no config surface, per the `commitments` precedent `{ disableTools: true }` in heartbeat-runner)
- **`SubagentRunParams`** (`plugins/runtime/types.ts`): `disableTools?: boolean`
- **`server-plugins.ts`**: forward flag into `AgentRunRequest`
- **`AgentRunRequest`** (`agent-request-types.ts`): `disableTools?: boolean`
- **`agent-run-execution-phase.ts`**: pass to `AgentCommandIngressOpts`
- **`AgentCommandOpts`** (`command/types.ts`): `disableTools?: boolean`
- **`attempt-execution.ts`**: `disableTools: opts.modelRun === true || opts.disableTools === true`

**Security:** the flag is intentionally absent from the external `AgentParamsSchema` — external callers cannot set it (`INVALID_REQUEST`); only the internal plugin subagent runtime can.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (live sandbox)

Sandboxed gateway (isolated state dir) + mock OpenAI provider logging verbatim request bodies:

- **BEFORE** (normal run, same sandbox): `tools` array with **26 entries**, total request **72,072 chars**, `tool_choice: "auto"`.
- **AFTER** (`disableTools` path): **no `tools` key, no `tool_choice`**, total request **366 chars**.

Honest scope note: the managed dreaming cron's registration proved timing-sensitive in the sandbox, so the live capture exercises the flag via the `modelRun` trigger (the **same** embedded-runner branch this PR extends), while unit tests prove `dreaming-narrative.ts` sets `disableTools: true` on its runs. Remaining unchecked: an end-to-end cron-fired narrative on a live gateway — happy to supply if wanted.

## Quantified impact (local-model installs)

Measured: tools payload 72,072 chars ≈ **~18K tokens** (chars/4 heuristic). On a measured local reference box (Strix Halo / gfx1151 unified memory, 122B MoE via llama.cpp: prompt prefill ~200 tok/s measured via ~100K-token cold prefill in ~7m49s; generation 15–25 tok/s):

| | tool construction (host) | tool-schema prefill | narrative prefill + generation | total vs 60s wait |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **before** | ~57s cold (measured on ARM, #93756) | ~90s (18K tok ÷ 200 tok/s) | ~25–45s | far past the 60s `NARRATIVE_TIMEOUT_MS` (#101603) |
| **after (this PR)** | skipped | 0 | ~25–45s | near/under the wall |

Three narrative phases per night → several minutes saved per sweep on local installs, and materially less KV/context pressure (#95746). Note the after-column still brushes 60s on modest hardware — this PR **composes with** the configurable timeout in #78440 rather than replacing it. (Estimated figures labeled; tool-surface size varies by install — MCP-heavy setups are worse than 26 tools.)

## Considered alternative: keep tools for prefix-cache sharing

Retaining the tool block so narrative runs share a KV-cache prefix with other run types was considered and rejected: (1) the host-side bundle-tools construction cost is unaffected by any server-side cache; (2) cross-run-type cache hits need byte-identical prefixes, which narrative runs break early anyway (distinct narrative system prompt/bootstrap context); (3) the caching that does occur in practice — the three narrative phases sharing a prefix with each other within a sweep — survives this change with a smaller shared prefix; (4) for per-token cloud providers the unused tool block is strictly wasted spend. No-tools is better for both deployment classes.

### Test plan

- [x] `dreaming-narrative.test.ts`: 30/30 (TDD — red first, then green)
- [x] `server-plugins.test.ts`: 72/72 (includes forward + external-schema-rejection coverage)
- [x] Typecheck (`run-tsgo`) clean; `git diff --check` clean
- [x] Live sandbox: 26 tools / 72,072 chars → no tools / 366 chars
- [ ] E2E cron-fired narrative on a live gateway (see scope note)

Refs: implements #93756 review guidance · context #92494 · composes with #78440 · should relieve #95746

target.title: fix: generated image previews return unauthorized
target.body:
Closes #106700

- AI-assisted: yes
- Maintainer edits: enabled

## What Problem This Solves

Authenticated Control UI generated-image previews can return `Unauthorized` when backed by `/api/chat/media/outgoing/...`. This change resolves session-bound preview/download through authenticated `artifacts.download`; unauthenticated direct HTTP remains rejected.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Proposed authorization contract: existing `operator.read` artifact scope; explicit Gateway-owner confirmation remains required.
- Managed URL, artifact session, stored record, transcript reference, and coordinates must all match.
- Direct HTTP retains its separate owner/admin requirement.
- `managed-image-artifact-coordinates` prevents newer UIs from enabling this coordinate-aware path against older gateways.
- No paired-device HTTP credential path, protocol version, config, migration, or plugin API change.
- Resolver and HTTP handler remain runtime-lazy.

## Files Touched

- `src/gateway/managed-image-attachment*.ts`: storage, parsing, validation, transcript binding, HTTP serving, and tests.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/artifact-download.ts` and `artifacts.ts`: lazy, read-scoped managed-byte resolution.
- `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-hello.ts`: additive coordinate-aware server capability.
- `ui/src/pages/chat/*`: authenticated preview resolution, capability gating, connection lifecycle, cache cleanup, reload behavior, and tests.
- `packages/gateway-protocol/*`, generated Swift protocol model, and `docs/gateway/protocol.md`: coordinate and capability contracts.

## User Impact

- Read-scoped authenticated Control UI users can preview generated images after all bindings pass.
- Unauthenticated HTTP and cross-session, stale-record, stale-transcript, or coordinate-mismatch requests remain rejected.
- Newer UI plus older Gateway preserves the prior path instead of enabling an unsupported resolver.

## Risks / Mitigations

- Security: local bytes return only after session, record, URL, transcript, and coordinate validation; Gateway-owner scope confirmation remains required.
- Version skew: UI requires the explicit additive server capability and artifact methods.
- Lifecycle: connection changes dispose the resolver and revoke cached object URLs.
- Generated contracts: Swift `ArtifactSummary.contentIndex` is synchronized with the TypeScript schema.

## Evidence

### Exact Head

- Commit: `3121f861e75`
- Base used for the current-main adaptation: `c69a75f6978`

### Exact-Head Review and CI

- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Max-lines repair extracted transcript binding and task-suggestion tests into focused modules without suppressions.
- Exact-head lint, production types, test types, docs, and CI gate: rerunning on GitHub.
- Fresh final-head autoreview: clean, confidence `0.99`.
- Earlier full branch autoreviews: clean after capability, generated-model, SQLite-store, and lifecycle fixes.

### Supporting Predecessor Proof

- Focused Gateway tests: `78` passed.
- Focused Control UI tests: `159` passed.
- Import-cycle check: `0` runtime cycles.
- Dead-export, changed-production-LOC, and targeted lint checks: passed.
- These results predate the final current-main adaptation and are supporting, not exact-head, evidence.

### Exact-Head Live Proof

A maintainer-authored Mantis request remains required. Before merge, add redacted authenticated Control UI preview and allowed/denied authorization evidence at `3121f861e75`.

### Prior-Head Live Proof (superseded)

At `f1279a66b8b`, Chrome rendered the preview, artifact RPC succeeded, unauthenticated HTTP returned `401`, authorized HTTP returned `200 image/png`, and source/download hashes matched. This is provenance only and does not satisfy the final-head proof gate.

## Maintainer Decision Needed

Should session-bound managed-image bytes returned by `artifacts.download` follow the existing `operator.read` artifact contract?

This head aligns the handler, protocol wording, UI capability path, and tests on `operator.read`. If the permanent contract must be `operator.admin`, those surfaces and visible UI recovery must change together before merge.

target.title: fix(macos): keep Canvas hidden for agent content operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who closed the Canvas panel would have it forcibly re-opened - with the app activating and stealing focus - whenever an agent touched canvas content. Every agent `canvas.evalJS`, `canvas.snapshot`, and `canvas.a2ui.push/pushJSONL/reset` re-presented the panel. The effect clustered right after gateway restarts/reconnects: the hosted A2UI page dies with the old gateway, so the next agent push always went through the re-present path, making closed Canvas windows reappear "on reconnect."

## Why This Change Was Made

Presentation was coupled to content access: `CanvasManager.eval`/`snapshot` and the node runtime's A2UI host ensure all routed through `CanvasManager.show`, which presents and calls `NSApp.activate(ignoringOtherApps:)`. This change separates the two: a non-presenting `ensureController`/`prepare` path owns surface creation and content loads, and only explicit intents (`canvas.present`, `canvas.navigate`, user actions) present the panel. Snapshot becomes strictly read-only: it requires an existing, matching, visible panel and returns `CANVAS_HIDDEN` otherwise, instead of mutating panel state. Named tradeoff: WebKit suspends rendering for ordered-out windows (hidden capture yields an unencodable image), so hidden snapshots fail fast with a clear error telling the agent to `present` first rather than popping UI for a read operation.

## User Impact

Closing or hiding the Canvas panel now sticks: agents keep updating content in the hidden panel, and it only reappears when the agent explicitly presents/navigates or the user opens it. No more Canvas windows popping up (and stealing focus) after gateway reconnects or during background agent work. Agents calling `canvas.snapshot` on a hidden panel get an explicit `CANVAS_HIDDEN` error instead of a surprise window.

## Evidence

- New `CanvasManagerVisibilityTests` (5 tests): eval on fresh state creates a hidden surface; `showDetailed` presents; content ops respect a user hide; hidden snapshot throws `CANVAS_HIDDEN` without presenting or leaving artifacts; cross-session snapshot leaves the live panel untouched.
- `swift test --package-path apps/macos --filter "CanvasManagerVisibilityTests|CanvasWindowSmokeTests"`: 10/10 passed on the rebased head.
- SwiftFormat 0 files require formatting; SwiftLint 0 violations; `git diff --check` clean.
- Structured autoreview (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`): final run clean - "consistently separates hidden content preparation/evaluation from explicit panel presentation, preserves the single-panel session behavior, makes snapshot semantics explicit and non-mutating."
- Docs updated: `docs/platforms/mac/canvas.md` documents the visibility contract.

target.title: fix(ui): sync agentSelection when switching sessions across agents
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

In the Control UI, switching from one agent's session to another agent's session via the session switcher updates the chat panel correctly, but leaves the left sidebar agent chip/select on the previous agent. Because the chip treats a re-click of the already-selected agent as a no-op, operators cannot return to the previous agent without a full reload or another workaround. The chat pane already syncs `agentSelection` from the session key; the sidebar and shell session-select paths did not.

## Evidence

Runtime before/after on the production selection contract (same `parseAgentSessionKey` + `agentSelection.set` sequence as `selectSession` / `selectChatSession`):

```console
$ node scripts/proof-session-switcher-agent-sync.mjs
BEFORE (setSessionKey only):
  sessionKey=agent:research:work
  agentSelection.selectedId=main
  agentId set called: null
  can re-select previous agent after switch: false

AFTER (sync agentSelection from session key):
  sessionKey=agent:research:work
  agentSelection.selectedId=research
  agentId set called: research
  can re-select previous agent after switch: true

RESULT: PASS — session switch keeps agent chip in sync
```

Source paths that now call `agentSelection.set` when the session key encodes an agent id:

- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar-session-navigation.ts` (`selectSession`, `replaceCurrentSession`)
- `ui/src/app/app-host.ts` (`selectChatSession` used by command palette + UI command navigate/split)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Session switcher / command-palette session selection updated chat `sessionKey` but not `agentSelection.selectedId`, so the agent chip stayed on the previous agent and re-clicking that agent no-oped (issue #109087).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS 15, Node v26.5.0, worktree `/tmp/oc-109087` on branch `fix/session-switcher-selected-sync` rebased onto latest `upstream/main`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

  ```bash
  cd /tmp/oc-109087
  node scripts/proof-session-switcher-agent-sync.mjs
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output from the live node proof script (above under Evidence). Before: selecting `agent:research:work` leaves `selectedId=main` so re-selecting main is a no-op. After: `selectedId=research` and the previous agent can be re-selected.
- **Observed result after fix:** Session switch now updates both gateway session key and agent selection, matching the chat pane `applyActiveSessionBindings` contract so the sidebar chip tracks the active agent.
- **What was not tested:** Full browser Control UI against a live multi-agent gateway (no live WebUI session in this environment). Sidebar/host controller coverage was run locally as a supplement outside this proof section.

## Summary

Closes #109087.

Mirror the chat-pane session-binding path: when a session key is selected, parse the agent id and set `agentSelection` before `gateway.setSessionKey` and navigate. Covers sidebar session rows, replace-current, command palette, and shell UI commands.

target.title: fix(agents): do not label finish_reason error as LLM timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When OpenRouter (or Google via OpenRouter) finishes a stream quickly with `finish_reason: "error"`, OpenClaw classified that completed provider failure as a timeout. Operators saw **LLM request timed out.** with `failoverReason: timeout` / 408-class signaling, even when `durationMs` was only a few seconds and `rawErrorPreview` was `Provider finish_reason: error`. That sends people to timeout/network knobs that cannot fix a provider-completed error. Model fallback still ran; the bug is mislabeling and bad diagnostics.

## Evidence

Production classifier modules on this branch (not a copied mock):

```console
$ pnpm exec tsx scripts/proof-finish-reason-error-not-timeout.mjs
BEFORE contract (expected failure modes without the fix):
  finish_reason:error matched ERROR_PATTERNS.timeout → reason=timeout, copy=LLM request timed out.

AFTER (production modules on this branch):
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"finish_reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"stop reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"Unhandled stop reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: network_error","reason":"timeout","isTimeout":true,"isProvider":false}
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: abort","reason":"timeout","isTimeout":true,"isProvider":false}
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: malformed_response","reason":"timeout","isTimeout":true,"isProvider":false}
  userFacing="Provider finish_reason: error"

RESULT: PASS — bare finish_reason:error is server_error, not timeout
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Bare `finish_reason: error` / stop-reason `error` was matched by `ERROR_PATTERNS.timeout`, rewritten to "LLM request timed out.", and classified as timeout/408 even for fast provider-completed failures (issue #109218).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS 15, Node v26.5.0, worktree `/tmp/oc-109218` on branch `fix/finish-reason-error-not-timeout` rebased onto latest `upstream/main`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

  ```bash
  cd /tmp/oc-109218
  pnpm exec tsx scripts/proof-finish-reason-error-not-timeout.mjs
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output under Evidence. Production `classifyFailoverReason` / `isTimeoutErrorMessage` / `formatAssistantErrorText` return `server_error`, not timeout, and keep the provider finish_reason string for operators. Abort/network/malformed finish reasons stay in the timeout lane.
- **Observed result after fix:** Provider-completed bare `error` finish/stop reasons are failover-eligible `server_error` with accurate user-facing copy; genuine transport hangs and network finish reasons remain timeouts.
- **What was not tested:** Live OpenRouter stream against a real key (no credentials in this environment). The production classifiers are the same functions the gateway uses on the agent-end error path.

## Summary

Closes #109218.

Remove bare `error` from timeout stop/finish patterns; add `isProviderCompletedErrorFinishReasonMessage` and classify as `server_error` before the timeout rewrite in `formatAssistantErrorText` and sanitize. Keep abort / network_error / malformed_response as timeout-like for #61281.

target.title: fix(telegram): bound miniapp auth rate-limit map with sweep and cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Telegram Mini App auth endpoint (`/__openclaw_tg_miniapp/auth`) rate-limits by client IP in a module-level `Map` (`extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.ts:27`). Entries were only overwritten when the *same* IP revisited after its window expired — there was no expiry sweep and no size cap. Every one-shot IP that ever POSTs to the endpoint (scanners, NAT churn, IPv6 rotation) leaves a permanent entry, so the map grows without bound for the process lifetime.

The replay cache in the same file already has both protections (`pruneReplayCache` + `REPLAY_CACHE_LIMIT`, `routes.ts:199-206`); the rate-limit map had neither.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `consumeRateLimit` now sweeps expired windows before consulting the map, then caps live entries at 1024 via the shared `pruneMapToMaxSize` helper (`openclaw/plugin-sdk/collection-runtime`), the same helper already used by line (`extensions/line/src/send.ts:50`) and mattermost (`extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/send.ts:82`).
- Because expired entries are swept before lookup, a renewed window is re-inserted at the map tail, so insertion order doubles as last-seen order and the cap evicts the stalest live entry first — never a recently active IP.
- The 1024 cap mirrors the sibling bounded rate limiter in discord activities (`TOKEN_RATE_MAX_KEYS = 1_024`, `extensions/discord/src/activities/rate-limit.ts:4`); the gateway's shared auth rate limiter (`createAuthRateLimiter`, `src/gateway/auth-rate-limit.ts:140`, used by the hooks request handler at `src/gateway/server/hooks-request-handler.ts:85`) likewise pairs a `maxEntries` cap with periodic pruning.
- Scope stays inside the telegram plugin: no shared API changes (`pruneMapToMaxSize` is already exported), no config surface added.
- Duplicate check: no open/closed PR covers this map; the only open Mini App PR (#110003) bounds auth request bodies, a different surface.

## User Impact

No behavior change for normal use: the per-IP limit (10 requests per 60 s window) is unchanged. Long-running gateways with the Mini App route enabled no longer accumulate unbounded per-IP rate-limit state. Worst-case eviction of a live entry merely restarts that IP's window (fail-open), the same tradeoff as the discord sibling limiter.

## Evidence

New behavior tests in `extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.rate-limit.test.ts`, driving the real HTTP route handler with distinct source IPs:

- **Cap**: 10 requests from one IP reach 429; after 1025 requests from distinct IPs the oldest entry is evicted and that IP gets a fresh window instead of a sticky 429. This test fails against unfixed `routes.ts` (verified via stash: 1 failed / 1 passed), confirming it reproduces the bug.
- **Sweep + recency**: with fake timers, an expired window revisited at 61 s restarts at the map tail; when the cap then evicts, the least-recently-seen filler is dropped while the recently active IP keeps its entry and is still rate-limited (429 on its 11th request).

Commands run (Node v24.15.0):

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.rate-limit.test.ts` → 2 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.test.ts` → 6 passed (existing suite, no regression)
- `git diff --check` → clean

Head SHA: `cab5c2a987817b02d284f0bc5f6e6ea6697e35d8`, based on `main` `8470a5befddd676d1a8379d44ce5fd6c268fa401`. Diff: 2 files, +144/-1 (`routes.ts` +12/-1, new test file +132).

target.title: docs: add ChromeOS (Crostini) platform install guide
target.body:
Closes #107662

_Drafted with AI assistance from my own Crostini install._

## What Problem This Solves

Users installing OpenClaw on a Chromebook have no ChromeOS-specific guidance. OpenClaw runs well inside the Crostini Linux container, but four gotchas differ from a plain Linux host and are easy to trip over:

1. Choosing the native install over Docker (Docker-in-Crostini can lose a container-home CLI login on rebuild).
2. Debian's default Node 18 being below the OpenClaw floor.
3. Provider keys not reaching the systemd **user** service when only `export`ed in a shell.
4. Crostini not being always-on across a ChromeOS reboot, so the Gateway silently stops.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a `docs/platforms/chromeos.md` platform page that mirrors the Linux guide's structure and documents the four gotchas, then wires it into the Platforms nav and cross-links it from the OS picker and the Linux page. Docs only — no runtime or config changes. The `~/.openclaw/.env` and `openclaw gateway restart` guidance matches existing docs (`docs/providers/meta.md`, `docs/tools/web.md`, `docs/gateway/configuration-reference`), and all internal links were verified to resolve to real pages.

## User Impact

Chromebook users get a clear install path and avoid the common failure modes: silently-missing provider keys, a Gateway that vanishes after a reboot, and a lost Docker-container CLI login.

## Evidence

- Set up OpenClaw on a ChromeOS/Crostini device this week and hit each of the four documented gotchas firsthand.
- Verified on the actual Crostini box that the Gateway binds loopback-only (`127.0.0.1:18789`), which is why the page does not promise browser access via `penguin.linux.test` (it would require rebinding off loopback) — that guidance was intentionally left out rather than guessed.
- Docs-only change; `git diff --check` is clean and every internal link resolves to an existing page. Docs link-lint runs in CI.

AI-assisted: drafted with Claude from my own Crostini install; I understand and verified the content.
